title: Romans 6:1–14
context: After justification, Paul answers “shall we continue in sin that grace may abound?” with baptism into Christ’s death and resurrection, dead to sin, alive to God, under grace.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on baptism into Christ’s death and resurrection, union with him, and walking in newness of life—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Romans 6:1–14.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Dead to sin—Freed both from the guilt and from the power of it. In baptism we, through faith, are ingrafted into Christ; and we draw new spiritual life from this new root, through his Spirit, who fashions us like unto him, and particularly with regard to his death and resurrection. We are buried with him—Alluding to the ancient manner of baptizing by immersion. As Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also, by the same power, should rise again; and as he lives a new life in heaven, so we should walk in newness of life. This, says the apostle, our very baptism represents to us. Our old man in a believer is crucified with Christ, mortified, gradually killed, by virtue of our union with him. Sin shall not have dominion over you—It has neither right nor power. Ye are not under the law—a dispensation of terror and bondage, which only shows sin, without enabling you to conquer it. But under grace—the merciful dispensation of the gospel, which brings complete victory over it to every one who is under the powerful influences of the Spirit of Christ.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Rom 6:2–14)

reformed.quote: The faithful are never reconciled to God without the gift of regeneration; nay, we are for this end justified,—that we may afterwards serve God in holiness of life. Christ indeed does not cleanse us by his blood, nor render God propitious to us by his expiation, in any other way than by making us partakers of his Spirit, who renews us to a holy life. We put on Christ in baptism, and we are baptized for this end—that we may be one with him. The death of Christ is efficacious to destroy and demolish the depravity of our flesh, and his resurrection, to effect the renovation of a better nature, and by baptism we are admitted into a participation of this grace. Ingrafting designates not only a conformity of example, but a secret union, by which we are joined to him. The Apostle does not exhort, but rather teach us what benefit we derive from Christ; he requires nothing from us which is to be done by our attention and diligence, but speaks of the grafting made by the hand of God.

verses.text: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the apostle here more fully vindicates his doctrine from the consequence suggested at Romans 3:7–8. He had then only denied and renounced it; here he removes the very foundation. The slander is that abundant grace makes continuing in sin reasonable.

Classical Arminians hear a real pastoral danger, not a hypothetical only one camp must answer. Grace that abounds is not a license. The question will be met by baptismal union and a walk that must actually be taken—not by treating holiness as automatic in the justified.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: those who imagine that gratuitous righteousness is given apart from newness of life shamefully rend Christ asunder. The flesh, hearing of justification by faith, invents this slander: if grace abounds where sin abounds, then sink into sin to find more grace.

Reformed reading: the objection is madness because Christ is the repairer of our righteousness. Medicine does not feed the disease it destroys. Justification never arrives without regeneration; the two are not separable gifts one might take and one refuse.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readings typically take the question as a live temptation under real grace: abundant mercy must not be twisted into license, and the baptized must actually refuse to continue. Reformed readings typically take it as a slander that rends Christ: gratuitous righteousness is never given apart from newness of life, so continuing in sin is not an option the regenerate might still reasonably choose.

verses.text: By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: dead to sin—freed both from the guilt and from the power of it. “By no means” is not a shrug; death to sin is real freedom. Yet “how can we still live” is the language of moral incongruity the believer must honor. Newness can be walked in or neglected.

Classical Arminians refuse to flatten “died to sin” into an irresistible state that cannot be betrayed. Baptism marks a real death with Christ; living in sin again would be a contradiction they are enabled not to enter—and still must not enter. The dead-to-sin life is a path, not a lock.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he who sins lives to sin; we have died to sin through the grace of Christ; then it is false that what abolishes sin gives vigor to it. The faithful are never reconciled without the gift of regeneration; we are justified that we may afterwards serve God in holiness of life.

Reformed accent: those truly dead to sin cannot remain in it as a reigning master. “How can we” is not a mere ought; it is the logic of effectual union. Christ does not cleanse by his blood in any other way than by making us partakers of his Spirit, who renews us to a holy life.
verses.keyContrast: Arminians typically hear death to sin as real freedom from guilt and power (Wesley) that must still be lived: enabling newness that can be walked in or neglected. Reformed readers typically hear effectual union: the regenerate have died to sin as a master and cannot live in its service; justification and regeneration are not separable.

verses.text: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: in baptism we, through faith, are ingrafted into Christ; we draw new spiritual life from this new root, through his Spirit, who fashions us like unto him, particularly with regard to his death and resurrection.

Arminian reading: baptism is not empty water. Through faith it marks real ingrafting—death with Christ as a lived participation. The “all of us” are those baptized into Christ, whose faith receives the union the rite signifies. The death is real; walking it out remains the believer’s calling.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: it is beyond question that we put on Christ in baptism, and that we are baptized for this end—that we may be one with him. We are then really united to his body when his death brings forth in us its fruit; this fellowship as to death is what is mainly to be regarded in baptism.

Reformed accent: baptism signifies and seals ingrafting. Paul, speaking of the faithful, connects the reality and the effect with the outward sign. When rightly received, the symbol is not naked; the Lord’s institution and the faith of the godly unite. Those so baptized are joined to his death in fact, not in emblem only.

verses.text: We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: buried with him—alluding to the ancient manner of baptizing by immersion. As Christ was raised from the dead by the glory (glorious power) of the Father, so we also, by the same power, should rise again; and as he lives a new life in heaven, so we should walk in newness of life. This, says the apostle, our very baptism represents to us.

Classical Arminians hear a grace-enabled path that must actually be taken. “Walk” is not a metaphor for what God does while we watch. Baptism represents death and resurrection; newness of life is the road the buried-and-raised must walk. It can be neglected. The same power that raised Christ enables the walk; it does not make the walking automatic.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the object of baptism into his death is that we, being dead to ourselves, may become new creatures. Fellowship in death and in life are tied by an indissoluble knot. Paul does not simply exhort us to imitate Christ as a pattern; he announces a doctrine: the death of Christ is efficacious to destroy the depravity of our flesh, and his resurrection to effect renovation, and by baptism we are admitted into a participation of this grace.

Reformed reading: this foundation laid, Christians may be exhorted to respond to their calling. The walk is the fruit of effectual union, not a condition that completes an unfinished burial. Those truly buried with him will walk in newness because God has joined them to the raised Christ.
verses.keyContrast: Arminians typically take “walk in newness of life” as a grace-enabled path the baptized must actually take—real burial and resurrection with Christ that can still be neglected. Reformed readers typically take baptism as signifying and sealing an effectual ingrafting: Christ’s death demolishes the old man and his resurrection renovates; the walk follows the union God has made.

verses.text: For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: surely these two must go together; so that if we are indeed made conformable to his death, we shall also know the power of his resurrection. The “if” is not a threat against union; it names a real conformity.

Arminian note: likeness of death and resurrection belong together for those indeed made conformable. The future “shall” is the promise of those who share his death—a path of dying to sin that resurrection-power accompanies. Certainty is for those who are indeed planted with him, not a guarantee irrespective of remaining in that death to sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: grafting designates not only a conformity of example, but a secret union by which we are joined to him; he, reviving us by his Spirit, transfers his own virtue to us. As the graft has life or death in common with the tree, we should be partakers of the life no less than of the death of Christ.

Reformed accent: great force in “ingrafted”: the Apostle does not exhort but teaches what benefit we derive from Christ. He requires nothing to be done by our attention and diligence, but speaks of the grafting made by the hand of God. Those united in a death like his shall certainly be united in a resurrection like his, because God has made the graft.

verses.text: We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: our old man—coeval with our being, as old as the fall; our evil nature; entire depravity spreading over the whole man. This in a believer is crucified with Christ, mortified, gradually killed, by virtue of our union with him. The body of sin—all evil tempers, words, and actions, the members of the old man (Col 3:5)—might be destroyed.

Arminian pastoral: crucifixion of the old man is real union, and it is gradual. “No longer enslaved” is the aim the believer must pursue. Mortification can be neglected; the crucified old man is not yet a finished corpse in experience. Grace enables the killing; the believer must walk in it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the old man is the whole nature we bring from the womb, incapable of the kingdom of God, which must so far die as we are renewed. He is fastened to the cross of Christ; by its power he is slain. We cannot be otherwise put to death than by partaking of his death. The body of sin is the corrupted mass.

Reformed accent: the end is that we may no longer serve sin. As long as we are children of Adam and nothing more, we can do nothing else but sin; grafted in Christ, we are delivered from this thraldom—not that we immediately cease entirely, but that we become at last victorious. Effectual union means the contest’s end is not in doubt.

verses.text: For one who has died has been set free from sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: he that is dead with Christ is freed from the guilt of past, and from the power of present, sin, as dead men from the commands of their former masters. Freedom is real: guilt gone, power broken.

Classical Arminians hear liberty that must be used. A dead man is not under a former master’s orders; a believer can still present members to that tyrant again (v. 13). Set free is enabling newness, not a lock that makes yielding to sin impossible. Walk as those who have been freed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: if death destroys the actions of life, we who have died to sin ought to cease from the actions it exercised. “Justified” from sin means freed from bondage. This work is not completed in a day; it goes on by daily advances. If you are a Christian, fellowship with Christ’s death must appear: the flesh crucified with its lusts.

Reformed comfort: the fellowship is not to be denied because relics of the flesh still live; its increase ought to be labored for. The reigning power is taken away and wielded by the Spirit. Those truly dead are set free from sin as master; remaining lusts are not remaining dominion.

verses.text: Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: dead with Christ—conformed to his death, by dying to sin. “We believe” that we will also live with him: faith looks toward a shared life. Dying to sin and living with Christ belong together.

Arminian reading: the “if” keeps conformity in view. Those who have died with him believe they will live with him—a hope to be walked in. Living with Christ is the promised counterpart of a death to sin that must continue. Belief here is the confidence of those conformed to his death, not a spectator’s certainty irrespective of remaining dead to sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: newness of life is to be pursued as long as they live; they ought to represent in themselves an image of Christ, crucifying the flesh once for all and carrying on the spiritual life continually. If we roll again in our own filth, we deny Christ; we cannot be participators except through newness of life, for he lives an incorruptible life.

Reformed accent: “we believe” denotes doctrine based on promises: the faithful ought to feel assured they are, through Christ’s kindness, dead as to the flesh, and that the same Christ will preserve them in newness of life to the end. The future “live” is the continued course of new life, not a maybe.

verses.text: We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Christ’s resurrection is once-for-all. Death’s dominion is broken over him; he does not cycle back under it. The pattern for believers is a life on the far side of death, not a return to the grave.

Arminian pastoral: “we know” is shared Christian confession. As his dominion-break is the ground of ours, so our living must match a Lord who does not die again. The knowledge is meant to be walked in. A believer who presents members to sin again acts against what is known of the risen Christ.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Christ, who now vivifies the faithful by his Spirit, was freed from death’s dominion when he arose, that by virtue of the same dominion he might render free all his people. He submitted to death’s dominion for a moment and destroyed it forever.

Reformed comfort: the risen Christ’s unrepeatable life is the life he breathes into his own. Those joined to him share a death that does not reassert its lordship. Dominion language here is the same as v. 14: the master who lost Christ will not keep those Christ has made alive.

verses.text: For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: he died to sin—to atone for and abolish it. He lives unto God—a glorious eternal life, such as we shall live also. Once for all: the atoning death is not repeated; the life to God is the life set before us.

Classical Arminians distinguish his death from ours without emptying the likeness. He died to atone and abolish; we die to sin’s guilt and power. The “once” calls us to a corresponding once of dying to sin, then a life actually lived to God. That life can be walked in or neglected; the pattern is clear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Christ is not said to die to sin so as to cease from it, as when applied to us, but that he underwent death on account of sin, that he might annihilate sin’s power and dominion. He died once, obtaining eternal redemption by one offering; and a mutual likeness exists: we die only once, when Christ, reconciling us by his blood, regenerates us at the same time by the Spirit.

Reformed accent: he lives to God in an immortal kingdom; a type of that life ought to appear in the regeneration of the godly. The new life we live on earth is similar to his celestial life. Union means his once-for-all death and his life to God become ours by the Spirit’s power, not by imitation alone.

verses.text: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Consider yourselves” is an imperative laid on the baptized. Reckon what is true—dead to sin, alive to God in Christ—and live accordingly. The reckoning is a grace-enabled act; it can be refused. Alive to God is the status of those in Christ Jesus; considering it is how they walk in newness.

Classical Arminians refuse to flatten the imperative into a mere announcement. Indicative union is real; the command to reckon is still a command. Believers can fail to consider, and so present themselves to sin again. The verse is pastoral: take the death and life as yours, and do not live against the union baptism marked.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: take this view of your case—as Christ once died to destroy sin, so you have once died, that in future you may cease from sin; you must daily proceed in mortifying until sin be wholly destroyed; as Christ is raised to an incorruptible life, so you are regenerated that you may lead a life of holiness, the Spirit’s power being eternal.

Reformed reading: “in Christ Jesus” expresses the grafting that makes us one with him. “Consider yourselves” is the indicative becoming the imperative because God has joined them to Christ. The life of sin is destroyed even though mortifying is only begun; spiritual newness continues perpetually. Except Christ slay sin in us to the end, his grace would not be sure.
verses.keyContrast: Arminians typically take “consider yourselves” as a sincere imperative: enabling newness the baptized must actually reckon and walk in—or neglect. Reformed readers typically take it as the indicative becoming the imperative: God has grafted them into Christ, so they count themselves dead to sin and alive to God because the union is effectual and the Spirit’s newness is durable.

verses.text: Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: let not sin reign even in your mortal body—it must be subject to death, but it need not be subject to sin. “Therefore” follows the reckoning: because you are dead and alive, do not let sin sit as king.

Arminian pastoral: the command is real because reigning is still possible. Mortal bodies still have passions; grace enables refusal. “Let not” is not theater. A believer can obey those passions again. The body will die; it need not serve sin while it lives.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: though sin dwells in us, it is inconsistent that it should be so vigorous as to exercise reigning power; the power of sanctification ought to be superior, so that our life may testify we are really members of Christ. Sin is original depravity; lusts are its edicts.

Reformed accent: “therefore” is ethics from union already established. The regenerate will not have sin as king. Dwelling is not reigning. The exhortation arises from fellowship with Christ; it does not imply that those truly dead to sin may still live under its throne.

verses.text: Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: neither present your members to sin—to corrupt nature, a mere tyrant. But to God—your lawful King. Two presentations: to a tyrant or to the King. The members are the same; the master is the choice grace enables.

Classical Arminians take this as the hinge of the chapter’s ethic. Baptized people can still present members as instruments of unrighteousness. “Present yourselves” is the walk in newness that must actually be taken. Brought from death to life is the ground; yielding to God is the required act. Neglect is possible; the tyrant will take whatever is offered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Christians ought to regard all their faculties as weapons of spiritual warfare; if they employ members in depravity, they serve sin. They have made oath as soldiers to God and Christ. Present yourselves wholly to God, ready to receive his commands. The Lord, having destroyed our former life, has not in vain created us for another.

Reformed reading: presentation to God is the reasonable service of those raised from death. The regenerate will present themselves, because they are no longer their own. The warning unmasks false claimants of the name; it does not teach that those truly brought from death to life remain free to re-enlist under sin as a lasting master.

verses.text: For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: sin shall not have dominion—it has neither right nor power. Not under the law—a dispensation of terror and bondage, which only shows sin, without enabling you to conquer it. Under grace—the merciful dispensation of the gospel, which brings complete victory over it to every one who is under the powerful influences of the Spirit of Christ.

Arminian hinge: “every one who is under the powerful influences of the Spirit” is not automatic possession irrespective of walking. Grace is the enabling regime; it is not dominion forced on those who present members to sin again. Under grace means the gospel gives power to conquer—power that must be lived in. Dominion is broken as right and as enabling; remaining under it is a refusal of that grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: a consolation, lest the faithful faint through consciousness of weakness. Their works are not tested by the strict rule of the law; God remits their impurity and mercifully accepts them. Not under the law means not subject to the law as requiring perfect righteousness and pronouncing death on all who deviate. By grace: both remission of sins and the sanctification of the Spirit, by whom he forms us anew unto good works.

Reformed comfort: however harassed by the stings of sin, it cannot overcome us, for we are enabled to conquer it by the Spirit; being under grace, we are freed from the law’s rigorous requirements. All without grace, bound under the law, are under condemnation; as long as they are under the law, they are subject to sin’s dominion. Those under grace will not have sin as lord.
verses.keyContrast: Arminians typically take “under grace” as the gospel’s enabling dispensation (Wesley: victory for everyone under the Spirit’s powerful influences)—newness that must be walked in, not a lock against presenting members to sin again. Reformed readers typically take it as effectual consolation: those under grace have both pardon and the Spirit’s sanctification; sin shall not dominate because God has formed them anew—the regenerate will live.
